blocks.text: Red teaming actively hunts for genuinely novel gaps in a system defenses, adopting an attacker mindset rather than checking against a predefined list of known categories, a creative, exploratory complement to the systematic security testing covered in the previous topic.

This topic covers adopting an attacker mindset, running structured red team exercises, using a model itself to help scale attack exploration, triaging findings by severity, and feeding genuinely novel discoveries back into the security test suite.
1. What Red Teaming Means
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473809112-58060318.png
Red teaming means deliberately trying to break a system defenses, approaching it the way a genuine attacker would, rather than simply verifying it passes a fixed, predefined list of known checks.
2. Red Teaming vs Systematic Security Testing

blocks.alt: Red Teaming vs Systematic Security Testing
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473809113-171710633.png

The previous topic covered running a repeatable test suite against known attack categories, red teaming instead specifically looks for what that predefined suite has not yet anticipated, genuinely novel framings, unexpected interactions between defense layers, edge cases no one thought to write a test case for.

blocks.text: 3. Adopting an Attacker Mindset
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473809113-187605629.png

This connects directly to the jailbreak and injection categories covered earlier in this module, but red teaming pushes further, genuinely asking, if I actually wanted to bypass this system defenses, what would I creatively try, rather than only checking whether known techniques still work.
4. Running Structured Red Team Exercises
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473809113-298208874.png

Effective red teaming is structured, not purely improvised, a defined scope, what parts of the system are in bounds to test, a reasonable time box, and a requirement to document every finding clearly, keeps the exercise productive and its results genuinely usable afterward.
5. Using a Model to Help Scale Red Teaming

blocks.alt: Using a Model to Help Scale Red Teaming
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473809113-557728165.png

This connects directly to multi-agent prompting, covered in an earlier module, using a separate model specifically tasked with generating creative attack attempts against the system under test can scale exploration far beyond what a human red teamer could manually attempt, functioning similarly to the generator and critic pattern but adversarially.

blocks.title: This does not replace human creativity, it multiplies it
blocks.content: A model assisting with red teaming can generate a large volume of attack attempt variations quickly, but a skilled human red teamer still contributes genuinely creative attack angles a model, trained to avoid generating harmful content itself, may not readily produce.

blocks.text: 6. Triaging Findings by Severity
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473809114-593397300.png

Not every red team finding carries the same urgency, a finding that bypasses a minor formatting constraint deserves far less priority than one that leaks sensitive data or bypasses a core safety instruction, triaging findings by actual severity focuses fixing effort where it genuinely matters most.
7. Feeding Findings Back Into the Security Test Suite

blocks.alt: Feeding Findings Back Into the Security Test Suite
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473809114-607122005.png

This connects directly back to the previous topic, once red teaming discovers a genuinely novel attack pattern, adding a corresponding test case to the systematic security test suite ensures that specific pattern gets checked automatically going forward, this is exactly how the two practices reinforce each other over time.
8. A Worked Red Teaming Example

A red team exercise on a customer support assistant discovers that a specific multi-turn conversation pattern, gradually escalating a hypothetical framing across several turns, successfully bypasses a safety instruction that held up fine against any single-turn version of the same request, a finding no existing single-turn test case in the security suite would have caught.
9. Red Teaming as a Periodic Practice

This connects directly to the arms race concept covered in the earlier Jailbreak Attacks topic, red teaming is not a one time exercise before launch, it needs to happen periodically, especially after significant changes to the system, since new attack techniques and framings continue to emerge across the field over time.
Worked Example

A team confident in their security test suite, which passes consistently against every known single-turn attack pattern, runs a structured red team exercise and discovers the multi-turn escalation pattern described above, a genuine gap their existing suite had no way to catch.

Adding a corresponding multi-turn test case to their security test suite, and adjusting their safety instructions to specifically address gradual escalation across turns, closes this gap, demonstrating exactly how red teaming discoveries feed back into and strengthen the systematic testing practice covered in the previous topic.
Common Mistakes

items: Treating red teaming as a one-time exercise before launch instead of a periodic, ongoing practice
Running red teaming without a defined scope or time box, making the exercise unfocused and its results hard to use
Discovering a genuine finding but never feeding it back into the systematic security test suite for future regression checking
Relying only on a systematic test suite and never attempting genuinely creative, exploratory red teaming at all

blocks.text: Practice

Pick a system you have designed or could design, spend fifteen minutes genuinely trying to think like an attacker rather than a defender, attempt at least one creative technique not already covered by a specific test case, and document what you find, even if the attempt does not succeed.
Key Takeaway

Red teaming actively hunts for genuinely novel security gaps by adopting an attacker mindset, running structured exercises, and optionally using a model to scale exploration, complementing systematic security testing by discovering what a predefined test suite has not yet anticipated, with findings feeding directly back into that suite as an ongoing, periodic practice rather than a one-time check.
